Section 1 — Executive Summary (1 page) — write last
Problem in one sentence, with the three measured baseline numbers (time, cost, error rate).

The proposed solution in one sentence, plus the headline feasibility finding (“a structured audit of 30 historical RFQs found X% of extraction fields technically automatable with current document-AI capability; a calibrated process simulation projects median cycle time falling from X days to Y hours”) — evidence-led, but honestly ex-ante.

Financial headline as a range, not a point: projected NPV (P10 / P50 / P90 from the Monte Carlo in 9.5), payback, and the floor case (“clears the hurdle rate on cost savings alone under conservative assumptions”).
The strategic claim: transaction data as the distributor’s future moat.
The actual recommendation — and this framing is critical: not “build the system” but
“approve a stage-gated pilot investment of € X, with explicit go/no-go criteria at each gate.”
An ex-ante paper that recommends a bounded, testable next step is far more credible than one that recommends a rollout.
Test: a professor reading only this page should know exactly what is fact, what is projection, and what decision you are recommending.

The RFQ from Innovo Contracting for Guggenheim Museum in Abu Dhabi lands at M.A.H.Y. Khoory's Abu Dhabi branch on Thursday evening, around 16:30. The scope is large, roughly 75 pumps across five applications, booster, transfer, sewage, circulation, and chilled water. The deadline is the following Tuesday. Innovo is a demanding client and this inquiry is no exception. Khoory is competing against Grundfos, Xylem, Wilo, and Lowara, and against at least one other distributor quoting the same Grundfos range Khoory carries, so this will be won or lost on service and price and speed of the quote as much as on brand.

The branch has two estimators. Properly working through an inquiry this size means reading every schedule and specification, checking material of construction, efficiency, pump orientation, and seal type, running head loss calculations for each application, going through the CAD files to confirm routing and layout, and running each selection through the manufacturer software. For 75 pumps across five applications this is close to twenty eight hours of estimating work. From Thursday evening to the Tuesday deadline is only three working days plus a weekend. Line managers bring both estimators in on Saturday and Sunday on overtime, and pull in a third from another desk, to try to close the gap. Even so, the volume is simply too much. Tuesday comes and the quotation is not ready.

The quote finally goes out to Innovo two days after the deadline, a full seven calendar days after the inquiry was received. Innovo's senior management escalates straight to Khoory's leadership, and a face to face meeting is needed to smooth things over. Khoory ultimately wins the project, but not on the strength of this quotation alone. The project brings a lot of back and forth given its size, and this is something we return to later in the paper.

: technical selection expertise, aggregation across manufacturers, credit, local presence. Plant the tension explicitly: “Each of these functions is under pressure from digitization; this paper examines what happens when the most defensible one — technical expertise — becomes automatable.” Do not resolve it here.

A distributor in this chain exists because the manufacturer cannot do what the distributor does, not economically, and often not at all. The first function is technical expertise. Every RFQ requires reading through consultant specifications, CAD files, and drawings, extracting flow, head, and efficiency requirements, running head loss calculations, and working out which specific model, across a manufacturer's full range, actually fits the site. For larger or more unusual applications, chilled water and booster pumps especially, this can mean going back to the manufacturer for a special quote before pricing the contractor. None of this is generic. A multinational manufacturer sells into dozens of regions, each with its own local requirements, consultant preferences, and site conditions, and cannot build that regional depth itself. That depth is what the distributor provides, and it is exactly the function that nearly failed under pressure in the Innovo inquiry.

The second function is credit. Multinational manufacturers are not set up to extend payment terms to individual contractors, many of whom carry project-linked terms, bank guarantees, and retentions that shift with each client's requirements. Rather than absorb that risk across dozens of contractors directly, the manufacturer works through one distributor and lets that distributor manage the market and the credit risk on its behalf.

The third function is local presence, which shows up mainly as after-sales service. Projects need testing and commissioning carried out by someone on the ground, and warranty and guarantee support that a contractor can actually call on when something goes wrong. Manufacturers rely on the distributor for this because contractors trust a local party they can reach, over a multinational head office they cannot.

Of the three pillars, technical expertise is the most expensive and the most time consuming to deliver. It needs trained estimators, manufacturer software, and hours of manual work per inquiry, and it is the pillar that broke down under pressure in the Innovo case. Credit and local presence are largely fixed costs of doing business in the market. Technical expertise is not; it scales directly with inquiry volume and complexity. That is why this paper focuses on it. The question is whether technical expertise, the reading, the calculations, the model selection, can be digitized without losing the judgment that makes it valuable.
The three measurable dimensions, each with a measured baseline number and its business consequence:
•    Speed → lost wins (evidence standard set in 4.6 and 9.3)
•    Cost → engineering capacity as the binding constraint on growth
•    Quality → error taxonomy preview (full version in 4.4)

A standard inquiry — three to twelve pumps across one or two applications — takes an estimator around five and a half hours of concentrated work: reading the specification and CAD files, running head loss calculations, selecting the model, and pricing it. The largest inquiries — several dozen pumps across multiple applications; the Innovo package ran to seventy-five — demand twenty-five to thirty hours of estimating effort and require pulling multiple estimators simultaneously, against deadlines sometimes as tight as two to three days. These large inquiries arrive roughly once a month but cannot be staffed as if routine. Timing costs real business: an estimated 15% of tenders are lost specifically to late or rushed quotes (E, sales and management interviews; treated as an upper bound and triangulated in 9.3), concentrated in two situations, smaller or first-time customers where there is no existing relationship to buy patience, and large fast-track projects landing while the team is already stretched on other work.

Khoory carries 16 estimators across all branches, each handling roughly 12 RFQs a week across the company's full product range. A fully loaded estimator costs the business approximately €22,000 a year. Hiring a qualified replacement takes two to three months, and a further three to four months before they are fully productive. Estimator capacity is therefore a hard constraint rather than a soft one: it directly determines how fast the business can take on new sales and new customers, independent of demand.

Errors are not rare. Across the 2025 quotation audit, roughly one standard inquiry in nine went out containing at least one defect — a wrong model, a wrong price, or a missed specification requirement — rising to one in five on the largest, most valuable work. The full error taxonomy and its cost consequences are developed in Section 4.4.
2.3 Research questions — reworded for the ex-ante frame
What process architecture could automate the RFQ process while preserving quote quality, and what evidence supports its technical feasibility?
What is the projected financial impact of the proposed transformation, and how robust is that projection under uncertainty?
What are the strategic implications for the distributor’s position in the value chain, and what implementation path best manages the risks?

The problems set out above, slow turnaround, hard capacity constraints, and error rates that erode margin and trust, are all downstream of the same underlying question: whether the technical expertise function of the distributor can be automated without losing the judgment that makes it valuable. This paper addresses that question through three research questions, each building on the last.

The first question, addressed in Sections 6 through 8, is what process architecture could automate the RFQ process while preserving quote quality, and what evidence supports its technical feasibility.
The second question, addressed in Section 9, is what the projected financial impact of the proposed transformation would be, and how robust that projection is under uncertainty.
The third question, addressed in Sections 10 and 11, is what the strategic implications are for the distributor's position in the value chain, and what implementation path best manages the risks.
In / out, one sentence of justification per exclusion. Add one explicit line:
“This study evaluates the proposed transformation ex-ante; implementation and post-implementation measurement are outside its scope and are addressed as a recommended pilot design in Section 11.”
Stating this once, early, inoculates you against the ‘but you didn’t build it’ critique — you convert the absence into a declared research design.

The scope is limited to pumps. Pumps are where the technical selection burden is heaviest, the Innovo inquiry alone required checking flow, head, efficiency, material, orientation, and seal type across five separate applications, and where the case for automation is strongest. Valves, HVAC, and other product lines Khoory distributes are excluded from this paper, though they represent a natural future extension once the pump-focused system is proven.

The scope is limited to the UAE. This is deliberate, not a data limitation: UAE is where the volume and the pain are concentrated today. GCC-wide expansion is excluded here but flagged as a near-term next step, since specifications and business practices across the wider GCC closely mirror the UAE market.

The scope covers the technical workflow from RFQ receipt through quote generation, reading specifications and CAD files, running calculations, selecting models, and pricing, and picks up again at the submittal stage, preparing and submitting technical documentation for consultant approval once a project is won. Explicitly excluded is the commercial negotiation between quote submission and LOI. This boundary is intentional: the paper automates the technical judgment function of the distributor, not the deal-making function, keeping the analysis aligned with the technical-expertise tension raised in Section 2.1.

This is an ex-ante evaluation. No software has been built, and no pilot has been run. The analysis instead relies on a calibrated simulation of the current process, an audited assessment of technical feasibility, and a defensible financial projection under uncertainty, developed in Sections 6 through 9. A live pilot is recommended, not conducted, and appears as the first stage of the implementation path in Section 11.
Section 3 — Methodology: An Ex-Ante Evaluation Design

the bracketed branch designation in 3.1 and the interview counts in Table 3.1 must be confirmed and completed with actual values. The scoping sentence reconciling the 640-inquiry baseline with Khoory's company-wide estimator figures is load-bearing — verify it reflects how the data was actually collected before submission.

This study is a prospective evaluation of a proposed process transformation — an ex-ante design, in the language of investment appraisal. Nothing described in Sections 6 through 8 has been built, and the paper makes no claim otherwise. What it claims instead is that the transformation can be evaluated to a decision-grade standard before a line of code exists, using the same discipline a rigorous organization applies to any capital investment: measure the current state, design the alternative from established components, model its behaviour, and subject the model's assumptions to structured challenge. The absence of an implementation is not a gap in the method; it is the method's defining condition, and the design below is built for it.
Four components carry the evaluation. The first is an
of the current quoting process — measured, not recalled — developed in Section 4 from inquiry records, direct observation and a quotation audit. The second is a

: the proposed architecture of Section 7, assembled from components whose individual behaviour is documented — foundation-model extraction, deterministic hydraulic calculation, the manufacturer's own selection tooling — so that the design's novelty lies in the assembly and the routing, not in any unproven part. The third is a

, in two connected models: a process model that projects cycle time and capacity under the proposed design, and a financial model that converts those projections into a probabilistic investment case (Sections 8 and 9). The fourth is

: the estimators who run the current process and the contractors who buy from it are used not as sources of enthusiasm but as adversaries of the design's assumptions, through the feasibility audit of 8.1, the design review of 8.3, and the contractor interviews of 4.6.

One scoping statement belongs here because every number downstream depends on it. Khoory operates 16 estimators across its UAE branches, each handling on the order of twelve inquiries a week across all the product lines the company distributes. The empirical baseline of Section 4 was measured at a single branch — [the Abu Dhabi estimation office] — whose 640 pump RFQs in 2025 constitute the study population, the slice of that workload within this paper's product scope; company-wide figures appear only where Section 9 scales the branch-level findings, and are labelled as such when they do. Measuring one branch deeply was preferred to measuring all branches thinly: the simulation of Section 8 needs step-level timings that only observation can supply, and observation does not spread.
Throughout the paper, every quantitative claim carries one of three tags, introduced in Section 4 and used without exception.
means read directly from records or timestamped observation of the current process.
means produced by the structured feasibility study of 8.1 — scored by the estimators against a written rubric, on real historical documents.

means an output of the process or financial model, traceable to a named assumption in Appendix A. The vocabulary is the paper's contract with its reader: at any sentence, it should be unambiguous which kind of knowledge is being offered.

Table 3.1 lists every source of evidence the paper draws on, what each supplies, and the section where it does its work. No other data enters the analysis. All monetary figures in this paper are stated in euros, converted from UAE dirhams at AED 1 = €0.23; the underlying records are dirham-denominated.

Two models do the projective work of this paper, and one rule governs both: a model earns the right to project a future it has not seen only by first reproducing a past that was measured.

represents the branch quoting operation as a flow of inquiries through the steps of Exhibit 4.1: arrivals by tier at the measured 2025 rates, touch times drawn from the observed step distributions, estimator capacity as the constraining resource, and queue behaviour matching the office's actual discipline — one owner per inquiry, first-in-first-out within an estimator's desk, interruptions for large inquiries modelled as pre-emption, since that is what the Innovo case shows actually happens. The model is built and run on the authors' operations-simulation platform, whose modelling approach and validation logic are described in 5.5. Before any to-be scenario is run, the model must reproduce the as-is baseline: median and P90 cycle time by tier, within a stated tolerance, against the measured values of Table 4.2. The calibration error is reported in 8.2 rather than buried — it is the number that separates simulation from arithmetic, and the reader is entitled to see it. Only then are to-be scenarios run, in which the automation-rate range established by the 8.1 audit replaces human touch time at the affected steps, and the model reports projected cycle time, estimator utilization and quoting capacity as distributions under low, central and high automation.

converts operational projections into an investment case by Monte Carlo rather than by point estimate, because the honest state of knowledge in an ex-ante study is a set of ranges. Three uncertain inputs dominate and are treated as distributions: the automation rate, bounded by the 8.1 audit; the win-rate uplift from faster quoting, bounded by the triangulation of 9.3 and deliberately floored at zero in the conservative case; and the build cost, bounded by the vendor-referenced estimates of 9.4. Sampling across these produces five-year NPV as a distribution — reported at P10, P50 and P90 with the probability of clearing the hurdle rate — rather than as a single number defended to false precision. Every input distribution is documented in Appendix C and traceable to its source through the Appendix A register; no parameter enters the model that the register does not name.

Three limitations are acknowledged now and treated fully in Section 12. The baseline is one branch of one distributor, measured over one year, and the deep-observation sample behind the step timings is 22 inquiries. The future state is simulated and audited, not observed: no live extraction accuracy, engineer adoption, or contractor behaviour has been measured, and the pilot recommended in Section 11 exists precisely to supply what this design cannot. And the demand-side evidence — how much speed is worth in won tenders — rests on triangulated history and stated preferences rather than experiment, which is why the financial model floors that benefit at zero before it claims anything else.

Author's note (remove before submission): all figures in this section are structured placeholders written to be replaced with the distributor's actual data. Volumes, times, costs and rates are internally consistent and realistic for a UAE pump distributor of this size, but they are illustrative until substituted. The (M) measured / (E) estimated tags mark the evidence standard each figure must meet once real values are inserted.

The analysis in this section rests on three sources. The first is twelve months of inquiry records drawn from the shared quotations mailbox and the quotation log — 640 inquiries received between January and December 2025 (M). The second is three weeks of direct observation in the estimation office, during which 22 inquiries were followed from the moment the email arrived to the moment the quotation left, with each handover and each period of waiting timestamped (M). The third is the finance ledger for credit notes, rework and warranty items traceable to quotation defects (M). Where a figure could not be read directly from these records, it was estimated from sampled data or from structured interviews with the estimation and sales teams, and is tagged (E) with the method noted. The distinction matters: everything the later sections project is anchored to what this section can demonstrate.
4.1 The as-is process: a swimlane view

An inquiry arrives as an email. Attached to it, in no particular order, will be some combination of a consultant's specification extract, a pump schedule — sometimes a native PDF, often a scanned image — a riser diagram, and occasionally a CAD file the estimator cannot open without asking a colleague. From that starting point the inquiry passes through nine steps and five roles before a quotation goes back out. Exhibit 4.1 maps the path, with each step annotated with two numbers: touch time, the minutes and hours in which someone is actively working on the inquiry, and queue time, the hours in which it sits in an inbox waiting its turn.

Exhibit 4.1. Median values across the 22 observed inquiries (M). The clarification loop and the management approval loop occur on a subset of inquiries; their queue times are medians within that subset.

The pattern the exhibit reveals is the central finding of the current-state study. Across the observed inquiries, the median case consumed 5.5 hours of actual work spread over roughly 39 working hours of elapsed time (M). Six hours out of every seven, nobody was working on the inquiry at all. It was waiting — first to be noticed and assigned, then in the estimator's personal queue behind whatever arrived before it, then, most expensively, on the contractor to answer a clarification, and finally for a discount to be approved by someone in a meeting. The work itself is not slow. The waiting is.
Exhibit 4.2. Touch and queue medians by inquiry tier (tiers defined in 4.2). The queue share is remarkably stable — between 86% and 88% — regardless of complexity (M).

Queue time is not evenly spread. Three steps account for most of it: assignment, where an inquiry waits a median of 14 working hours for an estimator to pick it up; the clarification loop, where the median wait for a contractor's answer is 41 working hours and the process cannot move until it comes; and pricing, where quotes above the discount threshold wait on a manager's availability. Each of these is a handover between people, and each handover is a queue. The cost side is more straightforward. At a fully loaded rate of €12 per hour — €22,000 a year spread over roughly 1,840 productive hours — applied to both estimation and sales time (E, from payroll and headcount records), the median inquiry carries roughly €66 of direct labour before any overhead allocation, a figure developed by tier in 4.3.

Treating 640 inquiries as one population would hide more than it reveals, because the inquiry that asks for a single replacement circulator and the inquiry that covers three buildings of a museum have almost nothing in common except the mailbox they arrive in. Every inquiry in the 2025 log was therefore classified retrospectively into one of three tiers using three objective criteria: the number of pumps requested, the completeness of technical data at the moment of receipt, and the project value. Two staff members classified independently; they agreed on 91% of inquiries, and disagreements were resolved jointly (E). The taxonomy carries through the rest of the paper — the design in Section 7 routes by it, the feasibility audit in Section 8 samples by it, and the financial model in Section 9 builds its benefits by it.
Chilled water, multi-building, special quotes to manufacturer
Table 4.1. Segmentation criteria and 2025 mix. n = 640 inquiries.

The inversion between the last two rows is worth pausing on. Tier 3 supplies one inquiry in eight but nearly half the quoted value, which means the inquiries that matter most commercially are precisely the ones where the manual process is slowest, the documents messiest, and the expertise thinnest — there are two estimators in the office who can handle a chilled-water package unassisted, and one of them handles most of them. Any redesign that only works for simple inquiries would automate the 12% of value that least needs help.
Table 4.2 consolidates the baseline. Every subsequent claim of improvement in this paper is a claim against one of these cells.

Table 4.2. Baseline metrics by tier, 2025. Cost per quote combines touch hours at loaded rates with a per-inquiry allocation of estimation software licences; defect rates were estimated by auditing a stratified sample of 120 quotations against source documents.

Three readings follow. First, cycle time grows faster than touch time as complexity rises — an 88-hour Tier 3 median contains only 11.4 hours of work — so the delay problem is structural, not a matter of effort. Second, the defect rate triples between Tier 1 and Tier 3, tracking the volume of manual transcription each tier demands. Third, and read together with the value shares in Table 4.1: the business earns its margin where its process performs worst. That tension is what the Innovo inquiry in 4.5 makes concrete.
4.4 Error taxonomy and the cost of poor quality

The audit of 120 sampled quotations, cross-checked against the credit-note ledger, surfaced four distinct classes of error. They differ not only in frequency but in when they are discovered, and discovery timing drives cost far more than the mistake itself: an extraction error caught at internal review costs an hour of rework, while the same error caught at commissioning costs a return shipment, a site visit, and a measure of trust.
Flow, head or model data mis-read or re-keyed wrongly from PDF, scan or drawing
Head-loss worked from wrong pipe length, material or fitting count; sizing off as a result
Feasible but wrong model — duty point at curve edge, wrong configuration for the application
Wrong list price, missed cost update, arithmetic in the discount line
Table 4.3. Error taxonomy from the 120-quotation audit and 2025 credit-note ledger. Categories are not mutually exclusive on a given inquiry; frequencies count inquiries where the class appears.

Summed across the year, the direct and traceable consequential cost of the four classes comes to roughly 1.2% of revenue (E). The chain matters as much as the total. Nearly every calculation and selection error in the sample began life as an extraction problem — a number read off the wrong riser, a scanned schedule transcribed by eye at the end of a long day. Attack the point of entry and much of the downstream taxonomy loses its supply.

The larger leak, however, never appears in an error report, because every individual instance of it looks like a reasonable commercial decision. Discounting at the distributor is set case by case, by whoever is pricing, without a reference point in front of them. Matching 2025 quotations on scope and value shows discounts on comparable Tier 2 work ranging from 4% to 18% (M) — not because the jobs differed, but because the days did. Interviews suggest the pattern: under deadline pressure, with the win uncertain and no anchor visible, the safe move is to give a little more away. Estimated against the median discount for like-for-like work, the foregone margin comes to roughly 1.9% of revenue annually (E) — half again as large as all four error classes combined, and invisible precisely because no single decision was wrong. Together, quality cost and discount leakage run to about 3.1% of revenue, and it is this figure the pricing engine in Section 7.5 is designed against.
4.5 The Innovo inquiry: Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, as-is

The numbers above describe the process in aggregate. One inquiry shows what they feel like from inside. On a Thursday at around 16:30, the Abu Dhabi branch received an email from Innovo Contracting, the pump package for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi development. The scope was large, roughly 75 pumps across five applications, booster, transfer, sewage, circulation, and chilled water, with a specification extract running to dozens of pages, pump schedules scanned as images, and riser diagrams covering several buildings. The contractor's own submission deadline was the following Tuesday.

By the criteria of 4.2 this was a large Tier 3 inquiry. Worked properly it needed close to 28 hours of estimating effort. The branch has two estimators. Line managers brought both in over the weekend on overtime and pulled a third estimator across from another desk to help. Even with three people and the weekend, the volume was too much to finish cleanly by Tuesday.

Table 4.4. The Innovo inquiry, timestamped from mailbox records and the estimators' logs (M). Touch total: 28 hours. Elapsed: seven calendar days, quote issued two days past the deadline.

Seven calendar days from receipt to quotation, and twenty eight hours of actual work spread across three estimators and a weekend. By the criteria of 4.2 this was a large Tier 3 inquiry, 75 pumps across five applications, and it landed well above the Tier 3 median in Table 4.2. What made it memorable inside the office was not that it was unusual. It was that the process simply could not absorb a job this size inside the deadline, however many people were thrown at it.

It also nearly went wrong. On one riser the static head was first read from the wrong drawing, an extraction error that would have undersized the booster set for the taller building, and it was caught only because the odd duty point prompted a second look. And the contractor's Tuesday reply sat unread for a stretch because nothing in the process flags a waiting inquiry when its answer arrives. Had either near-miss landed differently, the outcome would have been a defective quote on top of a late one, on a marquee project. Innovo's management escalated to Khoory's leadership over the delay, and a face to face meeting was needed before the relationship settled. Khoory eventually won the project, but the quotation itself was late, and it nearly went out wrong.

Compressing the evidence of this section — the swimlane timings, the tier metrics, the error audit, and the Innovo inquiry — yields four root causes, shown as a driver tree in Exhibit 4.3. They are worth stating separately because each demands a different remedy, and a design that fixes three while ignoring the fourth forfeits much of the gain.
Exhibit 4.3. Four root causes behind the observed cycle times, quality costs and margin leakage. Each maps to a specific element of the proposed design in Section 7.

Every technical fact the process needs arrives locked inside a PDF, a scan, or a sentence in an email, and is released only by an estimator reading and re-keying it. This is where 1.5 hours of every Tier 2 inquiry goes, and where 41% of defects begin. The Innovo near-miss was this cause in miniature.

One estimator owns an inquiry end to end, so work waits for a person rather than a task, and the scarcest expertise — two people for chilled water — sets the pace for the most valuable inquiries. The 84–87% queue share in Exhibit 4.2 is the signature of serial ownership, not of slow work.

Gaps in the data are discovered mid-process, one at a time, each triggering a round trip to the contractor at a median cost of 41 working hours — and nothing alerts anyone when the answer lands. Thirty-eight percent of inquiries need at least one loop (M); complex inquiries often need two.

Discounts are set without reference points, producing a 4–18% spread on comparable work and the largest single leak in the system. Unlike the other three causes, this one costs nothing in time — only in money, quietly, on jobs that were won.

These four causes are the requirements specification for everything that follows. The intake and extraction layer of Section 7 exists because of the first; confidence-based routing and parallel task design because of the second; automated completeness checks and clarification tracking because of the third; and the rules-based pricing engine because of the fourth. The current state, measured honestly, is the design brief.
4–6 contractor interviews: what drives supplier choice, how much speed matters vs. price, and — now doubly important —
their stated reaction to the hypothetical of an automated quote
. Because you cannot observe real behaviour toward the system, their stated preferences are your only demand-side evidence; gather them carefully and quote 2–3 verbatim.

Author's note (remove before submission): the works cited below are established literature in their fields, but every citation must be verified against the original source, page-checked where quoted figures appear, and formatted to the programme's referencing standard before submission. Subsection 5.5 is a deliberate placeholder pending documentation of the authors' simulation platform.

This paper draws on four bodies of work, and a fifth that grounds its method. Each is treated briefly and instrumentally: a source appears here only because a later section leans on it, and the rule adopted throughout is that anything cited in this section is cited again where it does its work. The review makes no claim to be comprehensive; it establishes what is already known so that the paper's contribution — an ex-ante case for automating one distributor's technical function — stands on ground rather than air.
5.1 Digitization of B2B distribution and the disintermediation debate

The oldest question raised by this paper is whether digitizing a distributor's core function hastens the distributor's own removal. Early electronic-commerce research answered yes: where markets move online, transaction costs fall and manufacturers deal directly with buyers, squeezing intermediaries out (Benjamin and Wigand, 1995). The counter-position emerged almost immediately — intermediaries do more than pass product, and new electronic forms of intermediation appear even as old ones dissolve (Sarkar, Butler and Steinfield, 1995). Chircu and Kauffman (2000) reconciled the two in a cycle they termed intermediation–disintermediation–reintermediation: incumbents that are displaced by digital channels can re-enter by absorbing the technology into the functions that made them valuable, provided they move before a substitute occupies the position. Two decades of practitioner research on wholesale distribution has broadly confirmed the pattern — distribution has consolidated and digitized rather than disappeared, with the gains accruing to distributors that made their differentiating capability digital first.

The relevance to this paper is direct. Section 2 identified three pillars that justify the distributor's position — technical expertise, credit, and local presence — and this study proposes to digitize the first. The IDR framing converts that from a tactical efficiency question into the strategic one Section 10 resolves: whether automating technical expertise makes the distributor the platform of record for its market, or merely writes the manual for its own replacement. The literature's answer is conditional on sequence, and sequence is a choice.
5.2 CPQ systems and their limits for engineered-to-spec product

Configure-price-quote software is the established commercial category closest to this paper's proposal, and its logic descends from the product-configuration research of the 1990s and 2000s: where a product family can be described by enumerable options and compatibility rules, a configurator can replace expert intervention in the sales process, and does so reliably (Forza and Salvador, 2002; 2007). Industry analysts define the mature CPQ category accordingly — guided configuration, rule-based pricing, and automated quote assembly on top of structured inputs.

The qualifier carries the weight: structured inputs. CPQ assumes the selling company already knows, in machine-readable form, what the customer needs; its intelligence begins after intake. Engineered-to-order environments violate that assumption at both ends — requirements arrive as drawings and specifications rather than option selections, and the mapping from requirement to product runs through engineering calculation rather than compatibility rules (Hicks, McGovern and Earl, 2000). A pump distributor's RFQ is a textbook instance: the flow, head, and pipework data that determine the answer are locked inside PDFs and riser diagrams, and the answer itself requires hydraulic computation no configurator performs. This gap is why Section 6 treats off-the-shelf CPQ as a component of the proposed design — it remains the right machinery for pricing discipline and quote assembly — rather than as an alternative to it. What the category has never solved, and what this paper's design must, is the unstructured front door.
5.3 AI document understanding: what the benchmarks do and do not promise

Because this study fields no prototype, published evidence on machine reading of business documents is load-bearing: it supplies the priors that the feasibility audit in 8.1 maps onto the distributor's own document mix, and it must therefore be reported with its flattering and unflattering sides intact. The flattering side is genuine. Layout-aware and vision-language models (Xu et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2022) have driven performance on the standard document-understanding benchmarks — DocVQA for question answering over document images (Mathew et al., 2021), FUNSD for noisy scanned forms (Jaume et al., 2019), SROIE and CORD for receipt-style key-field extraction — to levels that were out of reach five years ago, with the strongest current pipelines answering well above 90% of DocVQA items and specialist parsing systems reporting near-ceiling results on that benchmark.

The unflattering side is equally documented and matters more to this paper. Benchmark corpora are dominated by curated, single-genre documents — forms, receipts, clean scans — while recent evaluation work on enterprise extraction shows accuracy degrading sharply as target schemas widen and documents lengthen, with models that produce validly structured output still failing on correctness of the values inside it. Performance also varies materially across parsing pipelines and model versions, in both directions. The distributor's reality sits closer to the hard end of that spectrum: multi-column pump schedules scanned as images, specification extracts running to dozens of pages, units and symbols that differ by consultant. And one piece of arithmetic reframes even optimistic per-field accuracy: at 95% per field, a twelve-field schema is fully correct only about 54% of the time (0.95¹²). That arithmetic — not any distrust of the models — is why the Section 7 design carries per-field confidence scores, validation gates, and human review as structural features rather than as caution. The published ranges justify attempting extraction; they do not justify trusting it unexamined, and the audit in 8.1 exists to establish where on the published spectrum this distributor's documents actually fall.

Four decades of human-factors research warns that the failure mode of partial automation is rarely the machine's error alone — it is the human's changed relationship to the task. Parasuraman and Riley (1997) established the vocabulary of use, misuse and disuse: operators over-rely on automation that is usually right, and abandon automation that has embarrassed them, in neither case calibrating to its actual reliability. Automation bias — accepting a machine suggestion in place of one's own vigilance — produces measurable omission and commission errors even among trained professionals, as the systematic evidence from clinical decision support shows (Goddard, Roudsari and Wyatt, 2012), and it strengthens when the human feels less accountable for the outcome (Skitka, Mosier and Burdick, 1999). Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens (2000) supplied the design response: automation is not a switch but a set of levels applied per function, chosen deliberately.

The Section 7.6 routing design is an application of exactly these findings. Confidence is displayed rather than hidden, so the engineer's trust has something to calibrate against; uncertain fields arrive flagged rather than silently completed, forcing engagement where it is needed; release is an explicit act with a name attached, preserving the accountability that the bias literature shows keeps reviewers vigilant; and the level of automation is set per tier and per function, not for the system as a whole. The literature's uncomfortable implication is retained rather than argued away: a reviewer who approves ninety-nine good drafts is primed to approve the hundredth, and the value-gated release rules and override logging in 7.6 are the design's admission of it.

It is the oldest way of quoting pumps, and some distributors still work this way today. The engineer receives the RFQ and reads through the details like drawings, AutoCAD files, schedules, and specifications. It is all done manually to pull out the key details like flow, head, efficiency, material, orientation, and seal type etc. If something is missing, the engineer raises an RFI with the contractor, consultant or the manufacturer. With no selection software, the engineer opens the manufacturer's manuals and pump catalogues, reads the pump curves off the page, and picks the model by hand.

For a small number of simple inquiries, it works. But everything is manual, so the output depends entirely on how many engineers are available. It is slow, and it does not scale without hiring more people. Adding people is not easy. As shown in Section 2.2, a qualified estimator costs around €22,000 a year. It takes two to three months to hire one, and another three to four months before they are fully productive. So even when the business decides to scale, the extra capacity comes slowly and at a real cost. On top of this, the process is prone to errors that can happen at several points, like while reading the files, doing the calculations, and even during matching the curves by hand.

CPQ stands for Configure, Price, Quote. It is a category of sales software made to automate the commercial side of quoting. It assembles the line items, applies the pricing rules and discounts, handles approvals, and generates a clean quote document. It is good at the pricing and quote assembly end of the process.

The problem is that it solves the wrong end for us. CPQ is built for businesses with a smaller product basket, where the sales team already knows what to offer and just needs to put the quotation together. It cannot read an RFQ. 7.2 The to-be process: a projected swimlane

Exhibit 7.1 (Appendix B) mirrors the as-is map of Exhibit 4.1 lane for lane, with one addition: a System lane into which six of the nine steps migrate, running in minutes. The request fires within a minute of receipt instead of after the roughly 22 working hours of queueing and reading the as-is process needs (the 14-hour assignment median of 4.1 plus a day of reading), and when the reply arrives the layer recognises the thread, merges it, and resumes — closing the gap that left Innovo's answer sitting unread in a mailbox.

Extraction converts unstructured documents into one canonical record — a twelve-field-per-system RFQ schema covering identity, system type, flow, static head, pipe run, diameter and material, fittings, fluid, power supply and delivery date (Appendix G) — using language and vision models to read specification extracts, schedules and email text. Each field carries a confidence score, and it is these scores, not the values, that drive the routing of 7.7. One boundary is stated now: native CAD parsing is out of scope for Phase 1. 7.5 The product data layer: classification, storage and retrieval

None of the above works if the system's knowledge of pumps lives inside a language model. Models recall approximately; catalogues change monthly; and a quotation defensible under the audit constraint must rest on data that is exact, versioned and sourced. The design therefore separates reasoning from memory: models read documents and orchestrate, while a governed product database remembers.

Manufacturer data is normalized at ingestion into a four-level hierarchy — family, range, model, configuration — with each configuration carrying typed attributes in four groups: hydraulic (performance stored as Q–H, efficiency, power and NPSH point arrays or curve coefficients, never as prose), mechanical (materials, seal type, orientation, connections), electrical (voltage, phase, IE class), and commercial (list price, lead time, supersession chain). Attribute naming follows the ETIM classification standard for technical product data where the manufacturer supplies it, with a mapping table for house conventions — so that a model designation means exactly one thing to every layer of the system, and remains comparable if further manufacturers are added later.

Two stores, chosen by data type. Parametric and curve data sit in a relational database (PostgreSQL): feasibility questions — which configurations deliver 46 m³/h at 38 m head, in cast iron, at 400 V — are exact filters that must return the same answer every time, and SQL guarantees it. Unstructured technical content — specification sheets, application notes, installation constraints — is chunked, embedded and held in a vector index (pgvector, in the same database) for semantic retrieval when the reviewer or the clarification drafter needs supporting text. Curve data decides this architecture: selection quality depends on interpolating real curves, which is arithmetic on stored coefficients, not language.

The model never answers a product question from its own weights. It is granted tools — a structured query against the relational store, semantic search over the vector index, and the manufacturer's live selection API of 7.6 — and its outputs are schema-constrained, so any response naming a model must carry the database key and data version it drew from. Structured filters run first, semantic retrieval second: narrow, then read. Every record carries source and effective date, and each quote references the price-list and curve versions it used — which is what makes the constraint-three audit trail reconstructible months later, and keeps the system correct the week after a price revision. An ingestion pipeline from manufacturer feeds refreshes the store; a record that cannot name its source does not enter it.
7.6 Calculation and decision layer: three separated engines
Between a validated schema and a draft quote sit three engines, kept separate because they carry different uncertainty. The
hydraulic engine is deterministic physics, not AI

: total head is static head plus friction and fitting losses, computed by Darcy-Weisbach with Hazen-Williams as cross-check — the same formulas the estimators apply by hand, encoded once. Because this layer is settled engineering, its feasibility is not in question; the design's uncertainty lives entirely upstream in extraction, which is precisely what the Section 8 audit measures. The
selection engine is a constrained search

: given a duty point, it filters the 7.5 store, queries the manufacturer's selection API, and returns candidates ranked on efficiency, price and lead time, flagging duty points near a curve edge rather than accepting them silently [A5]; where several answers are defensible, the distributor's own history of chosen and winning selections breaks the tie — the data asset of Section 10, used here as a sort order. The
pricing engine is rules, not learning

: cost-plus by family, adjusted for customer tier and volume, with a defined discount band and a reference price beside every discount decision — aimed at the 4–18% spread and the 1.9%-of-revenue leak quantified in 4.4. Machine-learned price optimisation is deferred to Phase 3.
The preceding layers describe what the machine would do; this one decides what it is allowed to do. The routing is stated as logic:
IF   min. field confidence ≥ C₁ AND tier = 1 AND value < €V₁ AND discount in band
THEN auto-draft quote → engineer one-click release
ELIF tier ≤ 2 AND min. field confidence ≥ C₂
THEN engineer workspace: pre-filled schema, flagged uncertainties, ranked options
ELSE full engineer workspace + senior review (Tier 3, CAD-dependent, low confidence)

The thresholds C₁, C₂ and V₁ are design parameters, not findings; setting them against observed override rates is the work of the pilot in 11.1. Under this routing the estimator's role is redefined upward — exception-handler and consultative advisor, owning the flagged uncertainties, the curve-edge calls, and the Tier 3 work that genuinely needs judgement (change-management treatment in 11.2). What follows is a simulated scenario: the inquiry of Section 4.5 processed under the proposed design, with step times drawn from the Section 8 assumptions. Nothing in it has happened.

Thursday, 16:40: the email lands and intake opens it within the minute — classified, valued, in band [A1]. By 16:52 extraction has populated the schema and validation has found the same gaps a human found on day two, with the riser ambiguity flagged as an explicit conflict [A2]; at 16:53 a single consolidated clarification is on its way, thirteen minutes after receipt instead of 22 working hours [A3]. The contractor's reply is the one interval no redesign controls, so it is carried over at its measured pace: the request is seen on Friday and answered Monday morning. Within minutes of the reply the system has merged the thread, re-validated, run the head-loss calculations, filtered the product store, queried the selection API, and holds a draft quote — models ranked, the booster duty point flagged near its curve edge, prices in band. It is waiting on someone, rather than someone waiting on it. At 14:00 Monday, the estimator's first free slot, the review turns on the flagged selections; the senior's confirmation is two lines, one alternate is added, the discount stays in band [A6, A7]. At 15:10 Monday the quote would go out with the estimator's name on it per 11.3 — a day ahead of the deadline instead of two days late. Seven calendar days would become four; twenty-eight touch hours would become roughly [2.5–3, pending the Section 8 simulation] — the review of a 75-pump draft rather than its manual construction; and neither near-miss of 4.5 would arise to be caught. The design would be admitted in stages, each earning the next through a pre-defined gate. Phase 1 runs the pipeline in shadow, every quote human-released, outputs scored against the estimators — Phase 1 is the pilot itself. Phase 2 opens auto-draft for Tier 1 only, gated on extraction accuracy over N live inquiries, override rate below threshold, and zero escaped defects in shadow. Phase 3 makes assisted routing the Tier 2 default, auto-sends clarifications, and revisits deferred items — pricing optimization, CAD — on the strength of accumulated flywheel data, gated on Phase 2 metrics holding for a full quarter with adoption evidence per the 11.5 dashboard.
